notes.meaning: Amaziah took the throne of Judah at twenty-five years old and ruled for twenty-nine years from Jerusalem. Mentioning his mother Jehoaddan highlights his lawful royal line in David's family. He began his rule with the great advantages of youth, peace, and royal authority.

Amaziah did what was outwardly right in God's eyes, but his heart was not fully committed to the Lord. He supported temple worship and kept the law, yet he lacked sincere personal devotion and holy zeal. Outward religion without wholehearted love toward God leaves a person vulnerable to falling away.

Once Amaziah had firmly established his control over the kingdom, he executed the royal servants who had assassinated his father, King Joash. He waited until his throne was secure so that justice would be carried out properly and without rebellion. Bringing murderers to justice was a necessary duty for the king to restore public order.

Amaziah spared the children of the traitors, choosing to obey the law of Moses rather than common ancient customs that wiped out whole families. God's law taught that each individual must die only for their own sin, not for the sins of their parents. Obeying God's written word in this matter showed genuine moral courage and respect for justice.

Amaziah organized the men of Judah and Benjamin by clans and numbered all who were twenty years old and above fit for war. He found only 300,000 trained soldiers, a huge decline compared to the massive armies of earlier kings like Jehoshaphat. Past national sins and defeats had greatly weakened Judah's population and military strength.

Thinking his own army was too small, Amaziah paid one hundred talents of silver to hire 100,000 veteran soldiers from the northern kingdom of Israel. He sought to solve his shortage of men with money rather than praying and seeking the Lord's direction. Making ungodly alliances to gain human strength often creates problems that must later be undone.

A prophet came with a message from God, commanding the king not to take the hired northern soldiers to battle. The Lord was not with the northern kingdom of Israel because they had turned away to worship golden calves. Relying on partners who have abandoned the Lord brings danger rather than help.

The prophet warned the king that no matter how bravely he fought, God would make him stumble if he kept those hired troops. True victory does not depend on numbers, because God alone has the power to help or overthrow in battle. We must rely on God's strength alone rather than leaning on ungodly support.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Haydock explains that the prophet's words were spoken with irony, challenging the king to go ahead in his own strength to prove that Israel's ungodly aid could not save him.

notes.meaning: Amaziah worried about the large sum of silver he had already spent, asking what would become of the hundred talents. The prophet answered that the Lord is fully able to give him much more than what he had lost. When obeying God costs money or position, believers can rest assured that God can more than make up the loss.

Amaziah obeyed the prophet, parted with his money, and sent the northern mercenaries back home. The dismissed soldiers were furious, feeling insulted and cheated of the rich plunder they hoped to win from Edom. Obedience to God will sometimes stir up the anger of those whose only goal was worldly gain.

Taking courage from God's promise, Amaziah led his army south into the Valley of Salt near the Dead Sea. His troops struck down 10,000 Edomite warriors on the battlefield. God rewarded the king's obedience by giving Judah a decisive victory without the help of the mercenaries.

Judah's army captured another 10,000 Edomites alive and threw them down from the top of a steep rocky cliff, killing them all. This harsh execution reflected the brutal methods of ancient warfare used to crush rebellious enemies. While Judah won the battle, this severe cruelty displayed a spirit that lacked godly mercy.

While Amaziah was fighting Edom, the dismissed northern soldiers raided border cities of Judah, killing 3,000 people and carrying off great plunder. Their anger at losing the spoils of Edom was turned into violent vengeance against their southern brothers. God permitted this raid partly to discipline those border towns that had copied the northern kingdom's idol worship.

After defeating the Edomites, Amaziah brought back their carved idols, set them up in Jerusalem, and bowed down to worship them. It was total foolishness to worship the gods of a defeated nation that could not even protect their own people. Worldly success often blinds proud leaders into adopting the very sins that ruined their enemies.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critical commentators suggest the Chronicler created or highlighted this idolatry story to provide a theological reason for Amaziah's later defeat by Israel.

notes.meaning: The Lord was rightly angered by Amaziah's idolatry and sent a prophet to challenge him. The prophet asked why the king would seek gods that had just failed to save their own worshippers from Judah's hand. God graciously sends warnings and reasons with sinners before pouring out judgment.

Amaziah cut off the prophet in anger, asking who appointed him as a royal adviser and threatening to have him struck down. The prophet stopped speaking, but gave a final warning that God had determined to destroy the king for refusing to listen. Silencing God's messengers and hardening the heart against reproof is a sure sign of coming ruin.

Instead of seeking God's guidance, Amaziah consulted his court advisers and challenged King Jehoash of Israel to battle. He likely wanted revenge for the border raids and felt confident after his victory over Edom. Listening to flattering human counsel instead of God's word often leads rulers into reckless conflicts.

Jehoash answered Amaziah with a fable about a small thorn bush that demanded a marriage alliance with a stately cedar before being trampled by a wild beast. Through this story, the king of Israel mockingly warned Amaziah that Judah was weak like a weed compared to Israel. Proud people often imagine they are powerful giants when they are really in great danger.

Jehoash pointed out that defeating Edom had made Amaziah boastful and proud. He advised the king to stay at home rather than picking a needless fight that would bring disaster on both himself and his kingdom. Seeking unnecessary conflict out of wounded pride only invites sudden humiliation.

Amaziah refused to heed the warning, because God allowed him to follow his own stubborn impulses as judgment for seeking Edom's gods. The Lord handed Judah over to defeat to punish their idolatry. When people abandon God, He may leave them to their own foolish decisions to bring about their downfall.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Haydock notes that God permitted Amaziah to follow evil counsellors as a hardening of the heart that resulted from his earlier sins.

notes.meaning: Jehoash marched south with his army, and the two kings clashed at Beth-shemesh inside Judah's own borders. Because Amaziah had provoked the fight, his own people had to bear the devastation on their own soil. Rash challenges often bring warfare right to a nation's doorstep.

Judah's army was thoroughly routed by Israel, and every soldier fled back to his home in panic. Without God's presence and protection, Judah had no power to stand against their northern enemies. A nation that trusts in human pride will quickly scatter when testing comes.

Jehoash captured Amaziah at Beth-shemesh and marched him back to Jerusalem as a prisoner. The king of Israel then tore down a large four-hundred-cubit section of Jerusalem's defensive wall, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate. Amaziah's foolish arrogance left his royal city defenseless and exposed to shame.

Jehoash plundered all the gold, silver, and sacred vessels found in the temple under the care of Obed-edom's family, along with the royal palace treasures. He also took hostages to ensure Judah would not rebel, then returned home to Samaria. Forsaking God stripped Judah of its sacred treasures, wealth, and freedom.

Amaziah lived for fifteen years after King Jehoash of Israel died. Though he survived the war and regained his throne, his remaining reign was weakened by the loss of his army's honour and the city's defenses. Merely surviving for many years brings little joy when one lives under the shadow of spiritual failure.

The remaining events of Amaziah's life, from his early years to his end, were preserved in the royal annals of Judah and Israel. The record captured both his early obedience and his tragic turning away from the Lord. God ensures that every part of a leader's life and influence is faithfully remembered.

From the time Amaziah turned away from the Lord, his own subjects formed a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem. The king fled to the fortified city of Lachish for safety, but assassins followed him there and killed him. Turning away from God cost him the loyalty of his people and led to an untimely, violent death.

Amaziah's body was carried back to Jerusalem on horses and buried with his royal ancestors in the city of David. In spite of his tragic downfall and idolatry, he was granted a king's burial out of respect for God's covenant with David's house. God remains faithful to His covenant promises even when individual kings fail Him.
